header.title_plain: A different story about lactate: it's made by glycogen turnover feeding fast contractions, not by running out of oxygen
header.evidence_type: Review proposing the author's own "glycogen shunt" hypothesis, drawing mainly on NMR studies from his lab and a few others. No funding stated.

confidence.why: Contested hypothesis — a mechanistic hypothesis, not a settled model.

practical_relevance.why: Mechanism paper; the two coach-usable points (lactate is made in oxygenated muscle; carbohydrate feeding extends time to exhaustion) are background rather than programming changes.

header.author_stance: Proposes his own lab's hypothesis (the "glycogen shunt"), drawing mainly on NMR studies from his lab.

review.claim: Muscle contractions happen in milliseconds and need ATP on that timescale. PCr refills ATP within a single twitch, but something must refill PCr, and only glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) is fast enough. So glycogen is continuously broken down in milliseconds and rebuilt between contractions using oxygen. Lactate is the inevitable by-product of this fast, inefficient route — it is made in fully oxygenated muscle and is not a sign of oxygen shortage. Fatigue at low glycogen may reflect a failing rate of glucose flow through glycogen, not the glycogen level itself.

evidence_cited.finding: PCr swings within a single twitch
evidence_cited.source: Chung et al., rat muscle, 1-ms NMR
evidence_cited.numbers: PCr falls ~3 µmol/g per twitch (half-time 8 ms) and recovers (half-time 14 ms); whole cycle ~30 ms; ~40× more PCr use per twitch than the old slow method implied; ATP unchanged

evidence_cited.finding: Glucose can't supply it; glycogen can
evidence_cited.numbers: Free glucose + G6P in muscle <0.3 mmol — too little; ~1 µmol/g glycogen per contraction against ~70 µmol/g stores

evidence_cited.finding: Muscle without glycogen breakdown fails fast
evidence_cited.numbers: Resting pH ~7.2 vs 7.02 in controls; during exercise PCr falls much faster, pH stays high, patients can't sustain even mild exercise

evidence_cited.finding: PCr is not the whole story
evidence_cited.numbers: With <1% CK activity: shortening velocity −20%, max power −16%, work −30%, time to sustain −40%; force only ~20% down

evidence_cited.finding: Glycogen turns over even when its level is flat
evidence_cited.source: 13C NMR, human calf, 15/20/25% MVC for hours
evidence_cited.numbers: Glycogen settles at a lower plateau the harder the exercise; labelled glucose is incorporated into glycogen during exercise; 60% depletion after intense toe-lifts, then plateau not baseline

evidence_cited.finding: Carbohydrate feeding delays fatigue without sparing glycogen
evidence_cited.numbers: Fed subjects lasted 1 h longer; glycogen fell at the same rate in both groups; exhaustion at a similar, non-zero glycogen level

evidence_cited.finding: Oxygen is plentiful in working muscle
evidence_cited.numbers: Oxygen in working muscle falls with load but stays above mitochondrial needs even at VO2max

review.untested_or_contested: The twitch-level pH change was not statistically significant. The model rests on measurements that can't yet be made in whole-body human exercise. The author acknowledges the "normal physiological mechanism" for lactate production "has not been found" — this paper proposes one.

layer2.what_it_means: Two ideas a coach can use. First, lactate is not "the burn from running out of oxygen"; it's produced whenever muscle needs ATP faster than the oxidative route delivers, which happens in every hard contraction regardless of oxygen supply, and most of it gets re-burned as fuel. Second, hitting the wall at the end of long work may be about the flow rate of carbohydrate through muscle rather than the tank being empty — which is why feeding carbohydrate during long efforts extends time to exhaustion even though glycogen falls at the same rate.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: This is one lab's hypothesis built on rat twitches, a rare genetic disease, knockout mice and NMR of calf muscle at low intensity. It isn't a training study and it doesn't tell you how to train. The "glycogen shunt" is not consensus physiology; other models (e.g. Conley et al. in this batch) explain the same lactate without it. For a coach, the safe takeaways are the two above; the mechanism itself is for the curious.

translation: Lactate is produced in well-oxygenated muscle; it's fuel, not waste, and not a sign of oxygen debt.
Feeding carbohydrate during long hard sessions extends time to exhaustion (by ~1 h in the cited study).

glossary_candidates.definition: Breaking glycogen down into glucose units to make ATP fast.
Magnetic-resonance measurement of chemicals (PCr, ATP, glycogen) inside living muscle without a biopsy.
A genetic condition in which muscle can't break down glycogen; sufferers tire and cramp quickly.
The idea (Brooks) that lactate made in one place is carried to another and burned as fuel.
The enzyme that moves phosphate between PCr and ATP.
Maximal voluntary contraction; low-intensity exercise is often set as a % of it.
